newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee charges ahead, May, July set new high.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee charges ahead, May, July set new high.

text.p: CSCE coffee futures burst higher on Wednesday, with many contracts hitting new life-of-contract highs, as continued supply worries sparked a wave of speculative buying, traders said.
"The market perceives there is no coffee around," said Refco analyst Ann Prendergast. "And May's going through a squeeze because CSCE stocks are low and falling."

Today's rally was led by the spot May contract, which exploded to a new contract high of 240.00 cents per lb, before settling up a hefty 12.65 cents, to 239.05, its highest level on a continuous monthly basis since March 1, 1986.

Benchmark July arabicas surged 11.45 cents per lb -- or nearly six percent -- to close at 210.40 cents, after ranging between a new lifetime high of 212.00 and 200.40 cents. The back months closed 4.00 to 8.55 higher.
The May/July switch, a barometer of nearby availability, widened to 28.65 today from 27.45 at the close on Tuesday.

"The rest of the market is following May," said South Futures president Stephen Smith. "A lot of people were short May going into notice period hoping the market was going to come off. There's only 2,000 (lots) open interest, but there's no coffee in certified stocks."
Supplies of coffee certified for delivery against the exchange have dwindled steadily from a buildup of more than 83,000 60-kg bags three weeks ago.

The CSCE reported after Tuesday's close that certified coffee stocks fell another 1,500 bags, to 47,103 bags -- or about 188 lots -- as of April 28. Meanwhile, open interest on the May contract, which expires in less than three weeks, stood at 2,133 lots as of Tuesday's close.

After Wednesday's close, however, the CSCE reported certified coffee inventories increased for the first time since March 31. Stocks rose by 565 bags, to 47,668 bags as of April 29. There were 2,000 bags of coffee pending grading, the exchange said.

Many market participants expect tight supplies and the onset of the Brazilian winter to keep coffee prices well underpinned in the coming months. Smaller-than-expected harvests in many Latin American countries -- most notably second-largest producer Colombia -- and the prospect of a disappointing crop in top-grower Brazil in the 1997/98 season will also provide support, they said.
"If you're long, get longer. That's what the sentiment seems to be," said one trader. "In this kind of market, everything's bullish and feeds on itself."
But Refco's Prendergast said the market may be in for a setback once May goes off the board on May 19.
"I think its likely that July could go up to 220 or 225, but once delivery period is over it could lose ground," she said.
The day's volume reached an estimated 10,475 lots.
